CanonC3

A touchscreen controller for a Canon DSLR, run from a Raspberry Pi. Live view, full exposure control, a motion trigger that fires the real shutter, and an image-processing stack you program on the live feed.

display 800 × 480 touch
session labwc / Wayland
camera EOS Rebel T3 · 1100D
link USB · PTP · gphoto2
Manual · f/4.5 · ISO Auto · 1/60 · Single

Everything on the dial, under your thumb

Exposure strip

The top of the strip is the camera's settings: exposure mode, aperture, ISO, shutter speed and drive mode. Tap one to change it. What the camera reports is what the strip shows.

The yellow button

That's the shutter. Tap it for a frame, or press and hold in bulb for as long as you keep your thumb down. Full-resolution frames download straight to the Pi.

Top-right corner

Battery level, download everything on the card, connect the database (which feeds the web viewer), and quit.

AF / MF

Tap to focus. Drag to rack.

AF

Tap anywhere on the live view to autofocus on that point.

MF

Tap AF to switch it to MF, then drag across the live view to rack the lens: right moves focus nearer, left moves it farther. An on-screen readout shows the direction and step count.

Intervalometer

Set it, walk away

Shoot a sequence on a timer: a sunset, clouds rolling over, a night of stars. Pick how many frames and how often, press Start, and the Pi runs the camera while you get on with something else. The panel shows how far along the sequence is.

Frames

Anywhere from a handful to 999, or keep going until you press Stop.

Timing

One shot a second, one an hour, or anything in between.

Long exposures

Bulb mode holds the shutter open for up to an hour per frame, for star trails and night skies.

Noise reduction

Turn on the camera's long-exposure noise reduction for cleaner night frames.

Tip: the timer counts from the start of one shot to the start of the next. For a 30-second exposure with a 10-second break, set it to 40 seconds.

Motion trigger

Fires on the bird, not the breeze

An optical-flow detector watches the live feed on a worker thread and fires the real shutter when something moves across the frame. It follows motion over several frames: leaves swaying back and forth don't count, but something crossing the scene does.

Zone line

Drag a line across the scene to mark where movement counts.

Ignore regions

Draw regions over foliage, water or reflections to keep them out of the decision.

Scenes

Save the line and regions for a spot, like the feeder or the deck, and load them again next time.

HDR

One scene, several exposures

Shoots a bracket across shutter speeds, from dark to bright, so the shadows and the sky both survive when you merge them later.

Focus bracket

Sharp from front to back

Steps the focus between frames for stacking into one image that's sharp all the way through, which suits close-ups of flowers and insects. The focus_stack tool merges the frames afterwards.

Getting this to work on the T3 took some detective work. Three things we measured on the camera shaped it:

  • One file per sessionThe 1100D writes exactly one file per USB session. Later shots are accepted and write nothing. So each frame gets its own connect, shoot and disconnect.
  • No usable reverseStepping the focus back doesn't return it to where it was, so the sweep parks against the lens's hard stop and only ever steps forward.
  • Stop down for stacksOnly the coarse focus step is usable. Shoot at around f/11 so the depth of field in each frame overlaps the next.
Matrix

Every combination, one tap

Sweeps two settings at once, say aperture against shutter speed, and shoots every combination. Useful for learning a new lens, or when you're not sure which exposure a scene wants.

Split

Before and after, side by side

Shows the raw feed next to the processed output, so you can see exactly what a pipeline is doing to the scene.

Token pipeline

A Forth stack machine on the live feed

Type a pipeline as a row of tokens, read left to right. Source tokens push frames onto a stack, from now (t0) or seconds back (t-5), or as single channels. Operations pop frames and push results. Stateful tokens build up across frames, and camera tokens change a setting partway through. You can probe any token to see the stack at that point.

timechanunarybinarystackstatefulcamerapalette
t0t-5-absnormpalette-hot-iron

What changed in the last five seconds, drawn as a heat map.

grayastro

Faint-star stacking: a slowly fading maximum over the frames brings stars up out of the noise.

iso-800shutter-1/30t0bgsubmotion-capture

Set the exposure, subtract the background, and let the motion trigger shoot what's left.

Pipelines in motion

Some tokens remember: persist carries each frame into the next, so the picture becomes a record of time. Others are plain arithmetic on the current frame. These are screen recordings of the app running each pipeline on the simulator's test clips.

⬡ Print the picture

The ⬡ button on the pipeline bar turns the current frame into a 3D model: each pixel's brightness becomes a height, written as an STL you can spin in the web viewer or send to a 3D printer. A colour height map is saved alongside it as a PNG.

The ⏺ button on the pipeline bar records the processed output as a video. The palette tokens are standard DICOM colour tables from medical imaging, such as Hot Iron, PET, Thermal and Green Fire.

● Record

Movie mode from the Pi

Starts and stops the camera's own video recording. The app checks the camera's answer, not just the button press, so if the camera refuses (on the T3, the mode dial has to be on movie) you're told straight away instead of finding an empty card later.

⛁ Web viewer

Every trigger, frame by frame

Every session and every motion capture is logged, and a small web viewer running on the Pi lets you look back through them from any browser on your home network. There's nothing to install on your computer; just open the Pi's address on port 5000.

Sessions

Every time the app connects to the camera, that's a session: when it started, how long it ran, how many shots you took and how many times the motion trigger fired.

Captures

Each session lists its motion captures with the detector's score and a thumbnail of the trigger frame. Tap one to see every frame.

Pipeline gallery

Output from the token pipeline: colour-mapped images, videos recorded with ⏺, and 3D height-map models you can spin in the browser or download to print.

⏻ Run it

On the Pi, on your desktop, or with no camera

HostRaspberry Pi 4 with an 800 × 480 touchscreen, Pi OS, labwc / Wayland
CameraBuilt against a Canon EOS Rebel T3 (1100D) over USB
StackPython · PyQt6 · python-gphoto2 · OpenCV · NumPy
LoggingSessions and captures go to MariaDB. A Flask web viewer on port 5000 browses them.
DICOMOptionally sends motion captures to a DICOM storage server (off by default)
# kiosk on the Pi's touchscreen
$ bash launch.sh

# simulator: no camera needed, plays a sample video
$ bash launch.sh --sim

On your desktop

The camera stays plugged into the Pi, but the controller's window opens on your own computer, as an ordinary window you can drag around and use with a mouse. This is handy for setting up a scene from indoors while the camera sits by the feeder, or for working on a bigger screen. It runs over SSH on your home network, using X11 forwarding. Your computer needs an X server: Linux has one built in, and on Windows, WSL provides one.

# from your computer: open the Pi's controller in a window here
$ ssh -Y pi@canonc3.local
$ cd ~/CanonC3 && QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb .venv/bin/python main.py

Quit with the ✕ in the top-right corner. Killing the process can leave the camera's USB session open, and then the camera has to be switched off and on before it will connect again.
